criteria.evidence: Nameable as a navy-and-ice corporate cold-chain brochure: deep navy plus pale icy blue, a geometric grotesk headline, tracked-out numbered eyebrows like '01 / DOMESTIC', and a dark route-map panel.

In a desaturated view the headlines still dominate by size and weight, the navy bands still read as the darkest elements, and the filled buttons stay distinct from the outlined ones; nothing depends on hue to be read.

The 'What do you need to ship?' three-card row and the 'Your route' six-card route grid sit back to back and are the same device — bordered white cards with a small label, a bold title and an arrow link — and four sections share the same big-heading-left / small-paragraph-right header shape.
The hero is a left-aligned two-tone headline beside a real truck photograph carrying a dark caption bar reading 'FastWay refrigerated trucks / Our fleet and partner vehicles'.
A photograph of a Volvo tractor with a refrigerated trailer in FWL livery sits in the hero, and the FWL globe wordmark appears in the header and the footer.
The 'Our clients' row shows the actual Danone, Шин-Лайн and ХАМЛЕ marks as artwork, not typeset names.
'Get a transport quote' has From, To, cargo-and-quantity, temperature and date fields plus a submit button, and the FAQ rows expand.
Section headlines such as 'What do you need to ship?' and 'Your route. Our solution.' run genuinely large against very small letter-spaced labels like 'WHERE WE OPERATE' and '02 / INTERNATIONAL'.
The whole page is navy, ice blue and off-white; the only strong non-blue is the clients' own red logos. No violet anywhere.
The one illustrated panel is a labelled route diagram naming Kazakhstan, Russia, Europe, CIS countries and Central Asia — information, not an abstract shape; no glows or blurred blobs.
Zoomed in, the card icons are single-colour stroked line glyphs (snowflake, thermometer) in tinted rounded squares, plus a stroked phone and snowflake elsewhere — no emoji.
The brighter blue is confined to buttons, arrow links and the second line of two headlines; no section is washed in it.
Almost everything sits on one off-white page ground, with deliberate exceptions: two pale-blue inset panels (quote form, carriers) and one full navy band for 'How to book your shipment'.

Outside the cards there is only a rule-separated accordion, a rule-separated three-column band and a logo row; both the products section and the routes section, plus the fleet list, lean on the same bordered-card unit, and the card is the page's default answer to any group of items.
Copy names Kazakhstan, CIS and Europe, six specific route pairs, a phone number, WhatsApp as the channel, and placeholders like 'E.g. dairy products, 12 tonnes' and 'E.g. +2…+6 °C'.
No lorem and no statistics at all; the only placeholder text is inside form fields where it belongs.
The page closes on a carriers section — 'Have a refrigerated truck? Let's work together.' with 'Offer your truck' — a different audience and action from the header's 'Find a truck'.
Wide consistent gutters, a repeated left-heading column, and real breathing room around the navy band and the form; the spacing reads as a chosen rhythm rather than stacked defaults.
The trilingual switch, the WhatsApp-first submit, the local client marks and the route pairs are too particular to be a skinned template, even though the card-and-arrow vocabulary is common.
A studio would first fix the raw browser date field sitting in a custom form, the two identical snowflake icons on two different cards, and the unnormalised client logo row.

defects.what: A raw native date control — grey 'dd/mm/yyyy' text with the browser's own calendar glyph — sits inside an otherwise fully styled form, so the most important conversion surface on the page looks unfinished and styled by the OS rather than by the designer.
defects.where: 'Get a transport quote' panel, the 'When do you need a truck?' field

defects.what: The three client logos are dropped in raw at wildly different visual weights: a solid red ХАМЛЕ block, a red circular Шин-Лайн seal and a blue Danone mark, with no shared treatment (no single-colour or unified optical sizing). The red block pulls the eye off the navy page and the row reads as pasted assets.

Two different cards carry the identical snowflake icon — 'Chilled products' and 'Frozen cargo' — so the icons stop distinguishing anything and become decoration; only the third card gets its own thermometer glyph.
defects.where: 'What do you need to ship?' card row

defects.what: Two consecutive sections use the same compositional unit — bordered white card, small uppercase label, bold title, arrow link — so the page reads as one long card feed rather than a sequence of distinct moves.
defects.where: 'What do you need to ship?' followed by the 'Choose your route' grid

defects.what: The FAQ's entire left column holds only a heading and a phone number, and there are only three questions, so a wide region of the page carries almost no information while the right column stays thin.

The clients row places its heading, three logos and vertical dividers in one thin band with no supporting proof — no count of shipments, no relationship detail — so the strongest trust asset on the page is used at its weakest.

A counter reading '01 — 06' sits beside 'Choose your route' implying a carousel or a paged control, but all six routes are already visible in a static grid, so the counter promises an interaction that is not there.
defects.where: Header of the 'Choose your route' grid

defects.what: The hero headline breaks mid-phrase ('Need a refrigerated / truck?') and splits into two colours across two sentences, so the first line reads as an orphaned fragment before the eye reaches the question mark.
The route map mixes solid connector lines with one dashed line to 'CIS countries' and adds a faint orbital ellipse, with no legend saying what the dash or the ellipse means.
defects.where: Dark route-network panel in 'Your route. Our solution.'

defects.what: Three of the five quote-form fields are explicitly labelled 'Optional' in a small grey line under the label, repeating the word down the form and adding visual noise where a single note would do.

aesthetic_in_one_phrase: Navy-and-ice corporate cold-chain brochure — Swiss-ish left-aligned grid, geometric grotesk headlines, numbered eyebrows and one dark route-map panel
